Meet Michael Hyatt: The Underrated Canadian Founder
La IA ha generado este título a partir de la publicación a continuación.
Kai Thomas
10 meses
Denunciar esta publicación
The Most Underrated Canadian Founder You’ve Probably Never Heard Of
If Michael Hyatt were American, he’d have 500,000 LinkedIn followers, a book deal, and a Netflix documentary called “How to Print Money Legally.”
But he’s Canadian…
So nobody talks about him.
Let’s fix that.
Meet Michael Hyatt: the quiet Canadian who sold not one, but TWO huge companies before he turned 30.
Everyone knows Shopify.
Everyone knows Lululemon.
But almost nobody knows the guy who built one of Canada’s most valuable cybersecurity firms and sold it for $400M+, and then just kept going.
This is why I love studying founders like Hyatt:
They aren’t loud.
They aren’t flashy.
They just win.
The Story
At 17, he’s playing with servers while the rest of us were trying to get a date to grad.
At 25, he starts his first tech company, Dyadem.
At 29, he sells it.
Then he does the most un-Canadian thing ever:
He starts another one.
That company?
BlueCat.
The invisible plumbing behind the internet that no one thinks about until it breaks.
Think cybersecurity meets infrastructure meets “oh God don’t let this fail.”
Everyone said building it in Canada was impossible.
Hyatt built it anyway.
Scaled it.
Then sold it for hundreds of millions.
Instead of buying a yacht and disappearing to Anguilla, he becomes an angel investor, backs dozens of companies, becomes a CBC Dragon, gives straight-talk business advice, and mentors founders across the country.
No ego.
No influencer vibes.
Just results.
Why I’m Obsessed With His Playbook
Here’s the thing about Hyatt:
He didn’t build a social app.
He didn’t build a marketplace.
He built boring infrastructure that powers the internet.
And boring infrastructure is where the money is.
His lessons hit hard:
Solve real problems, “not founder feelings.”
Ignore hype, focus on customers who pay.
Build discipline, not dopamine.
Be relentless, even when nobody sees you.
Think decades, not quarters.
Canada desperately needs more founders like him, quiet killers who build important things instead of shiny things.
The Takeaway
Canada has a lot of amazing founders building amazing things.
They’re the ones who don’t go viral.
They don’t chase clout.
They build internet plumbing, cybersecurity rails, utilities, enterprise tools, the stuff billion-dollar companies rely on.
Hyatt is the blueprint:
Start small
Build something real
Sell it
Do it again
Help others
Simple.
Not easy.
If you’re building something in Canada, study this man.
He’s one of our country’s best founders.
We just haven’t built him a statue yet.

My First 4 Businesses Failed Badly…But Now I Run 2 Successful Companies. And Before I Ever Start a 3rd, These Are the First 5 Systems I Will Build
.
.
.
.
.
I used to think failure meant I wasn’t smart enough.
Or maybe I didn’t try hard enough.
Or maybe business just “wasn’t for me.”
But looking back, I realized one thing
My businesses didn’t fail because the ideas were bad…
They failed because they had no systems.
Every day felt like guesswork.
Sales depended on luck.
Operations depended on mood.
Money entered but never stayed.
And I was constantly solving problems that shouldn’t have existed in the first place.
When the business grows faster than the structure behind it,
failure becomes inevitable — no matter how talented you are.
So when I finally got it right — when I built businesses that don’t drain me, businesses that run with clarity and predictability — I realized something important:
If I ever start another business from scratch,
I’m not starting with branding, website, staff, or even the product.
I’m starting with systems.
Because systems determine whether the business survives, grows, or collapses.
Here are the first 5 systems I will put in place before anything else:
1️⃣ Leadership System
To define direction, decision-making, accountability, and culture.
Businesses don’t rise to the level of their goals — they rise to the level of their leadership clarity.
2️⃣ Operations System
So work becomes predictable, repeatable, and consistent.
Operations are the backbone. Without them, even the best ideas become chaos.
3️⃣ Marketing System
Not random posting, not inconsistent ads —
a system that constantly attracts qualified leads without stress or desperation.
4️⃣ Sales System
So conversions don’t rely on “talented salespeople,”
but on a clear, repeatable process that delivers the same result every time.
5️⃣ Finance System
Because a business can be busy and still be broke.
Finance systems protect you from silent failure — the kind you don’t notice until it’s too late.
The truth is:
My first four businesses didn’t fail because I was unlucky.
They failed because I was building energy, not systems.
Now?
I run two thriving businesses, and the difference is night and day.
Not because I became smarter…
but because I became structured.
And whenever I’m ready to build the third,
The systems come first.
How has building systems or lack of it affected your business?

Exit-Ready Without Exiting: Why Every Founder Should Build Like They’re Selling
Most founders I talk to have no plans to sell their business. They’re building for the long haul, maybe passing it to family someday, or just running it profitably for years.
So why do I keep telling them to get “exit ready”?
Because exit readiness isn’t about selling. It’s about building a business that runs without you constantly holding it together.
What Exit-Ready Actually Means
An exit-ready business has three things:
- Clean, auditable financials
- Documented systems and processes
- Operations that don’t depend on the founder’s daily presence
These same things make your business more valuable, easier to scale, and frankly, less exhausting to run.
The Real Benefits (Even If You Never Sell)
You can take a vacation. If your business falls apart when you’re unreachable for two weeks, you don’t own a business you own a job.
You can raise capital. Banks and investors want to see proper financials and documented processes. Whether you need equipment financing or growth capital, exit-ready businesses get better terms.
You can hire senior talent. Good executives want to join companies with real systems, not just founder intuition and “we’ll figure it out.”
You have options. Life changes. Health issues happen. Family priorities shift. An exit-ready business gives you flexibility to step back, bring in a partner, or yes sell if circumstances change.
Where to Start
Get your books clean. Personal and business expenses separated. Monthly financial statements you can actually trust. A chart of accounts that makes sense. This isn’t optional, it’s foundational.
Document your processes. The stuff only you know how to do? Write it down. Client onboarding, supplier relationships, quality checks, problem escalation. Start with the things that would break if you were gone.
Build management layers. You don’t need a full C-suite, but you need people who can make decisions without you. This might mean a strong operations manager, a reliable bookkeeper, or a sales lead who owns the pipeline.
Create a real org chart. Even if it’s just five people. Clear roles and reporting lines make it obvious where gaps exist and what needs to change as you grow.
The Test
Ask yourself, “Could someone competent run my business for three months with minimal input from me?”
If not, you’re not exit ready. You’re also probably exhausted.
The Bottom Line
Building an exit-ready business isn’t about planning to leave. It’s about creating something sustainable, scalable, and honestly sane to operate.
You might never sell. But you’ll sleep better knowing you could.

Cleaning up your inner world is a huge business growth lever.
So I turned it into a simple clean-up process I use on repeat.
Most founders don’t think about this.
I didn’t either until I noticed something strange:
my business bottlenecks weren’t operational, they were internal.
I’ve worked with founders at every stage and I’ve watched this pattern repeat:
the ones who scale cleanly aren’t just strategic, they’re emotionally uncluttered.
For me, it showed up quietly.
No big breakdown or dramatic pivot.
No “I moved to Bali and found myself.”
Just this constant low-grade friction.
Decisions took longer than they should.
I second-guessed offers I knew were good.
There was a subtle heaviness around visibility, pricing, and rest.
(Why did raising my rates feel like I was asking for a personal favor?)
So instead of adding another tool, I did something else.
I started clearing.
Not my inbox.
My inner environment.
Much more difficult, but much stickier.
And that’s when things moved.
So I turned it into a framework I now use for myself and with clients:
The Inner Clean-Out Method
☞ Name the leaks
Where does your energy consistently drain?
Look for patterns.
The hesitation before posting. The sigh before client calls.
The resentment you keep justifying.
☞ Separate truth from inheritance
Ask: Did I choose this belief, or did I absorb it?
Urgency culture, rest guilt, fear of being seen. Most of it isn’t yours.
☞ Install boundaries before strategy
Before refining your offer or funnel, decide:
What am I no longer available for?
Misaligned clients love a boundary-free environment.
☞ Clear one internal rule
“I must be liked.”
“I can’t slow down.”
“I need permission.”
Delete one and watch decisions suddenly require fewer Google Docs.
☞ Replace, don’t leave empty
Clearing without replacement creates wobble.
Install something intentional: trust, spaciousness, self-respect, patience.
Chaos will try to move back in if you don’t.
After doing this, here’s what changed:
I decide faster.
My offers feel cleaner.
My pricing feels anchored.
Clients feel easier to say yes to.
Creative momentum returned without force.
I’ve seen the same shift in founders who stop trying to optimize around their internal noise,
and finally address it directly.
Are you avoiding the emotional mess underneath your business?
To your becoming,
Claire Marie ♥

The most dangerous moment in a new business isn't the launch.
It's month three.
When the initial energy runs out. When the first strategy doesn't work. When you're alone at your laptop realizing nobody taught you this part.
20% of new businesses fail in year one, but the decisions that kill them happen in the first 90 days. Not the big, dramatic ones. The quiet ones.
What to charge. Who to trust. Whether to pivot or push through.
These aren't failures of effort or intelligence. They're failures of isolation.
Here's what nobody says: The career ladder didn't disappear. It was pulled up. And millions of people—solo consultants, first-time founders, people who never planned to be entrepreneurs—are now building in mid-air.
They're told to "move fast and break things."
But when you're building alone, breaking things means breaking yourself.
We're entering an era where technology's job isn't to make us faster. It's to make us less alone in the decisions that matter.
Not AI that writes your emails. AI that pressure-tests your pricing before you send the proposal.
Not tools that automate tasks. Tools that act as the second opinion you don't have access to.
The question isn't whether independent work is the future. It's already here.
The question is whether the people building alone have the same probability of success as the people building with infrastructure, advisors, and safety nets.
Right now, they don't.
We're working to change that.
If you're building something alone right now—a practice, a product, a business you never imagined starting—you're not imagining the risk. It's real.
But so is the possibility that you don't have to do it blind.

Madison Dearborn Partners, LLC ("MDP") is a leading private equity investment firm based in Chicago that, since its formation in 1992, has raised aggregate capital of approximately $31 billion and has completed over 150 investments. MDP seeks to invest in partnership with outstanding management teams to drive growth and achieve significant long-term value appreciation at its portfolio companies and for its limited partner investors globally. He retired from video games in October 2012, with his third “career chapter” at ThresholdImpact, where he focused on sustainable, profitable impact investing: mentoring and angel investing in information technology, new media, and medical innovations with social entrepreneurs. An active angel investor and entrepreneurial mentor, Dr. Muzyka is a member of the Young Presidents’ Organization, the A100, the Ashoka Support Network, and the Board of Governors of the University of Alberta (serving as Chair of the Human Resources Committee and on the Learning and Discovery Committee and as a member of the University of Alberta Advancement Council). He additionally was named as the 2017 Allard Chair in Business at the MacEwan University’s School of Business and as an Honorary Paul Harris Fellow by Rotary Club International in 2016, in recognition for his philanthropic efforts. Other awards include entry into Canada’s Top 40 under 40 and Ernst and Young’s 2001 Entrepreneur of the Year (IT, Prairies).He obtained his Bachelor of Medical Science from the University of Alberta in 1990, his Doctorate of Medicine from there in 1992, and his MBA from the University of Western Ontario (Ivey School of Business) in 2001.

Workwolf
— Workwolf is a recruitment services company that combines human recruiters with proprietary AI and psychometric technology to deliver predictive hiring intelligence at disruptive pricing. The company addresses a fundamental inefficiency in the $150B+ recruitment industry: traditional agencies charge 15-25% of candidate salary for subjectiveassessments with no performance accountability. Workwolf’s technology-enabled model delivers measurable quality improvements at significantly lower cost per hire. The proprietary technology platform includes two core components: Smart Resume Screening for contextual qualification matching, and Packfinder™ psychometrics for role-specific performance prediction. Show Notes
Serial tech entrepreneurs who have built successful companies time and again have deep knowledge and expertise. When you can get them to open up and reveal their secrets to success it’s a great opportunity to learn. In this episode, Ben Wilde interviews Michael Hyatt, the founder of BlueCat Networks and Dyadem, as well as a well-known investor and speaker, and one of the hosts of the TV show Dragon’s Den. Find out what it takes to succeed in today’s cut-throat tech world. You'll hear about: -Working on your strengths and partnering for your weaknesses (3:35) -The importance of hiring big egos and letting your people make decisions (4:20) -Why autonomy and purpose are the keys to retaining top talent (6:48) -How to hire the right people (8:13) -Why tech companies need to be able to pivot (10:35) -The characteristics of great board members (13:04) -Some of Michael's biggest missteps and lessons learned (15:57) -The difference between good and great products (19:06) -The importance of security as a fundamental product feature (21:28) -Emerging opportunities in the life sciences(22:52) -Why you should and shouldn’t be worried about technology (26:13) -Why humans are bad at predicting the future (29:20) -The massive opportunities yet to emerge online (31:16)

By BlueCat Networks (Sponsored Post)
IP Address Management (IPAM)
March 30, 2011
Views: 12,125
BlueCat Networks, the IPAM Intelligence™ company with over 1,500 clients worldwide, has received the highest rating given to vendors in the Gartner authoritative “MarketScope for DNS, DHCP and IP Address Management (IPAM), 2011”* report.
In the MarketScope report, Lawrence Orans, a research director in Gartner’s Research organization, notes that “IPAM applications offer a range of capabilities for controlling, automating and managing the domain name and address space, and these tools are a significant improvement over spreadsheets and homegrown address management applications.” Further, “Gartner estimates that the DDI market generated approximately $216 million in 2010, representing a 23% increase over 2009. They estimate that the market will grow another 28% in 2011, to approximately $276 million.”
“We are thrilled to receive this ‘strong positive’ rating from Gartner based on an expert evaluation of our IP Address Management, DNS and DHCP solutions,” said Michael Hyatt, CEO and co-founder of BlueCat Networks. “We believe our momentum is unmatched in this report and it is proof that the investments we have made in our products and in our world-class support and professional services organizations are exactly what the market wants. BlueCat Networks’ success in winning several large deals, along with its strengthened distribution channel and solid organic growth, are powerful testaments to our product and business strategy.” Hyatt continued, “The proliferation of IP-enabled devices, as well as strategic initiatives such as virtualization and private clouds, are driving the adoption of IPAM solutions. BlueCat Networks is uniquely positioned to help organizations improve the manageability, resiliency and efficiency of their networks and, as a result, we are showing up on more ‘short lists’ of Gartner clients.”
To pre-order a complimentary copy of the Gartner MarketScope report, please visit: www.bluecatnetworks.com/gartner.

It depicts Gartner’s analysis of how certain vendors measure against criteria for that marketplace, as defined by Gartner. Gartner does not endorse any vendor, product or service depicted in the MarketScope, and does not advise technology users to select only those vendors with the highest rating. Gartner disclaims all warranties, express or implied, with respect to this research, including any warranties of merchantability or fitness for a particular purpose.

From Roommates to Co-Founders: The Story of Building & Selling a Successful Toronto-Based Tech Company — Sampford Advisors - Expert Tech M&A Advisor (Software, IT Services, SaaS, Hardware)
From Roommates to Co-Founders: The Story of Building & Selling a Successful Toronto-Based Tech Company
Let’s rewind all the way back to 1997. Two guys just enrolled at the University of Waterloo to study Computer Science. They became roommates. What eventually took place is a series of exciting and challenging moments, cool experiences, and invaluable lessons that anyone can learn from. Below is the story of Ravin Shah and Tishan Mills and their successful start-up QuickTapSurvey.
Ravin and Tishan graduated in 2002, shortly after the dot-com bubble had burst. Given the volatility in the economy, most people in their cohort took shelter in secure jobs with stable companies. For Ravin and Tishan, the excitement of starting something on their own took precedent, but getting to that point took some time, and some trial and error.
Ravin moved to Chicago and started working as a consultant for Accenture. He then worked for Lehman Brothers for a year before coming back to Toronto. Tishan did his Masters of Applied Science after finishing his bachelors and then worked for companies like IBM, Sapient, and RBC in their technology divisions.
They were always entrepreneurs at heart, but were just waiting for the right idea and the right time.
In 2009-2010 both Ravin and Tishan began seriously exploring the possibility of starting something. The mobile revolution was taking off, specifically with the introduction of the iPhone and later the tablet. And then, there was a defining moment. One day, as Ravin and Tishan were walking down the street, they were stopped by someone holding a clipboard asking if they could be surveyed on a topic. Noticing the hassle of using a paper-based technique was the tipping point both of them needed to ignite the spark of creativity. This exact moment gave birth to TabbleDabble (aka QuickTapSurvey).
--
To uncover the story of QuickTapSurvey, I sat down with Ravin and Tishan to learn about how they met, why they started the Company, what they did to grow the business, and their eventual decision to sell/exit.
Making it through the Valley of the Shadow
Reid Hoffman, internet entrepreneur, venture capitalist, and author (Co-Founder of LinkedIn) said “entrepreneurs can have, as part of their plan, the desire to become famous, cool or rich, but they do have to be driven by something more. 99.99% of all startups go through a Valley of the Shadow – where they think why did we think this was a good idea? Why did we think this was going to work?”
[George]: Did you go through the shadow?
[Ravin/Tishan]: Oh yeah. We felt that shadow every month for the first year! It was a deep shadow and even though you see the light, it’s definitely difficult for start-ups to get over that hump – especially ones that are bootstrapped. Funding was much more difficult to secure 8 years ago than it is now so not only did we have to get over that shadow, we had to do it in a very resourceful way.
[George]: What was the most difficult part of that experience?
[Tishan]: What made it difficult was the fact that we were investing our own money into this company, our own savings. On top of that, we were both not getting a salary in the first 2 years. To make things more interesting, my son Nathan was born – so I had a child, a mortgage, a family, and being an entrepreneur didn’t make it comforting at first. That was my personal shadow.
[George]: So what made you stick with it?
[Ravin]: Optimism. Time isn’t on your side when you’re building a business from scratch, so we had to keep pushing it on and what made a difference for us were small wins. During the journey, we had small wins that would provide the necessary motivation and money to unlock the next month…a few of those happened in succession to buy us enough time to stick with it.
[Tishan]: The other thing that was challenging is when we launched our product in 2012, we had little revenues at first, but the ball started rolling from there – we thought we’ll get to the 2014 mark in the first year so our expectations were off in terms of what it actually takes to grow a business.
Having the right partner(s) can make or break your success
According to Steve Hogan, Managing Director at Tech-RX (a Silicon-Valley based venture capital firm), the #1 thing failed start-ups have in common is that sole founders don’t have partners. Contrary to the popular misconception that entrepreneurship is a lonely road, a crucial factor to start-up success is aligning yourself with an all-star team that complement the gaps you have.
[George]: What roles did you take on in the beginning and how did you split them amongst yourselves?
[Ravin]: I was definitely more geared towards the sales and marketing aspect of the business – anything to do with client success. That being said, I didn’t really know the “sales process” that well either – things like following up, knowing your buyer, having a call to action, etc. weren’t as intuitive so I ended up spending lots of energy in the beginning doing things that were less effective.
[Tishan]: I guess we figured it out over time. It’s funny though because in the beginning, we would explain the business to a VC and they would be a little weary of our team as they would think Ravin and I were both computer science guys leading the management team. Eventually, we both fell into roles we naturally gravitated towards – Ravin was sales, marketing, customer experience and I was technology, product development, engineering, QA, etc.
[George]: What do you like most about having a Co-Founder?
[Ravin]: You can have vacations. No, seriously – it makes a huge difference to have someone as your backup, someone you can trust and is fully capable of running the business while you’re not there.
[Tishan]: It also helps to have someone who understands what you’re going through. That moral support is a big factor because as we’ve said before, when you’re going through that valley of the shadow and everything’s on the line, you can have that partner/friend to talk to and lift you up again.
[Ravin]: Also, even though we were friends, we still set formal rules and standards from the beginning. We even went as far as setting how many vacation days we can each take and that meant holding ourselves accountable to a company we had to grow/scale. Those conversations were awkward at first, especially because we were friends, but it’s better to have them upfront in the beginning to lay out what’s acceptable and what’s not.
[George]: When did you start feeling reassured about the success of the company?
[Ravin]: When we started paying ourselves a salary. When Tishan and I started working on QuickTapSurvey full time, we had no other choice but to make it a success – financially. Again, because we were bootstrapped, we had to think about profit from day one and it was a continuous process for us where the more we made, the more we would reinvest in the business.
[Tishan]: We moved into a tiny one-room office in Scarborough and as the company grew, we just started growing the space as well (expanding into other rooms within the building). Once the company started making real revenues, we not only grew in office space but in size of the team as well – that was super important to us as Co-Founders because we were essentially the ‘Chief Everything Officers’ for a long time.
Knowing when it’s the right time to do the right thing
Michael Hyatt, Co-Founder of BlueCat (which was sold for $400 million to a US firm) said that “entrepreneurs should be thinking about building a great business, and exits come from companies who run great businesses.”
[George]: At what point did selling the business become a consideration?
[Ravin]: We had calls showing interest in the company at many points of the journey, but we ignored most of them. Then, at one point, we started getting more calls and there seemed to be a larger interest in the market – seeing as though the market was hot and buyers were on the lookout we started to pay more attention to a potential exit.
[Tishan]: We were also product-focused tech founders who scaled the company to a certain level, and to take it to the next jump required different skillsets. At the point where we started thinking about a sale, we also had different options on the table like continuing to grow the business, but we figured that doing so would also mean absorbing more risk – and our families deserved some security.
[George]: What was the feeling like when you closed the sale?
[Ravin]: Sense of relief. It’s really an emotional rollercoaster when you’re going through the process because there are a lot of unknowns – being unsure of whether it’s going to work or not, going through the due diligence, the negotiations, etc.
[Tishan]: Once the pen touched the paper to sign/close, there was a sigh of relief – the goal was accomplished.
[George]: What are you looking forward to most now that it’s done?
[Tishan]: Definitely advising/mentoring some companies, and maybe starting another company sometime in the near future.
[Ravin]: Spending time with family, taking some time off, and getting recharged for the next venture!
[Ravin/Tishan]: All in all, its really been a fun ride, we learned so much through this process, and experienced a ton.
Key Takeaways
Expect the Valley of the Shadow - growing your business will be more challenging than you think
Stay optimistic and focus on small wins - A positive attitude and early success will allow you to stick with it longer
Profit is King - working on your bootstrapped start-up full-time, making a profit is a priority from day one
The “Foundation” Team - Find the right partner you can trust, and who has skillsets that complement your gaps
Build it RIGHT and they will Come - Focus on building a successful business first, and a successful exit will follow as a result

About Event
​Canada is at an inflection point. In this private session, join Michael Hyatt (DataStealth) and Dan Debow (Build Canada) for a candid conversation about how today's founders and operators can build, hire, invest in, and find their edge in Canada.
Important Note: This event is by invite only. You will be required to share more information about yourself in order to be accepted to join the event. Only those who receive approval will be admitted on the day of the event.
We are officially part of Toronto Tech Week 2025, a weeklong citywide collection of events to connect and celebrate the builders. June 23 → June 27, 2025 | torontotechweek.com.
​About our Speakers:
​Michael Hyatt is a serial entrepreneur and investor. He co-founded BlueCat, which was acquired by Madison Dearborn Partners in Chicago, IL, and Dyadem, acquired by IHS (NYSE: IHS). Presently, Michael serves as a Senior Advisor at Northleaf Capital Partners and shares his business insights as a commentator on CBC. Michael was also a Founding Partner at the prestigious Creative Destruction Lab (CDL) within the Rotman School of Management.
Michael holds the role of Executive Chairman at DataStealth.io, an enterprise cybersecurity firm that allows organizations to discover, classify, and protect their most sensitive data and documents, ensuring that sensitive data and documents are secure and that they meet applicable privacy, regulatory, governance and compliance requirements.
Beyond business, Michael is active in philanthropy, leading the Hyatt Family Foundation. The foundation's primary areas of focus encompass women's health, critical hospital research, and support for underprivileged minorities.
​Daniel Debow is a Founding Member of Build Canada and a former VP of Partnerships and Corporate Development at Shopify.
Daniel was previously CEO and founder of Helpful, a startup backed by Bessemer Ventures that was acquired by Shopify in 2019. Prior to that, Daniel was SVP, Emerging Technologies at Salesforce and co-founded Rypple, which was acquired by Salesforce in 2011. Prior to Rypple, Daniel was VP Marketing & Corp Dev for Workbrain, which was acquired by Infor in 2007.
​Daniel is an early investor in over 50 technology companies. In 2015 he was recognized as Canada’s “Angel Investor of the Year”. Daniel holds a JD/MBA (Gold Medalist) from the University of Toronto, an LLM from Stanford University and a BA (Psych) from Western University.

Telemedicine. Telemedicine. And you know, the guys that, uh, a great VC in Toronto called Portage has, has a really good telemedicine. They bought that years ago. Uh, I think telemedicine is awesome. I think, um, um, uh, anything that's pushing a digital transformation logistics, like everything you just said, I, you know, I'm not sure I'm on the boat of, you know, still buying into Peloton, those type of work from home, be home stuff. I think it's going to get a lot more intense in 2021 and 2022 around how healthy are you? Um, can you get on an airplane? Can you do this? documents.title: Tank Talk w/ Michael Hyatt (Hyatt Family Office) - Being a Family Office During the Crisis

context.quote: So I'm Michael Hyatt. I'm an investor and entrepreneur. I founded a few companies, I sold a few companies, and I spend my time with our family office and our our foundation
context.claim: In his own account, Hyatt is an entrepreneur and investor who founded and sold multiple companies and now spends time with his family office and foundation.

context.quote: I invest in private equity companies, venture capitalists. I direct angel invest in real estate. We buy a lot of stocks and that kind of stuff. we just a general purpose investing
context.claim: Hyatt describes a general-purpose investment approach spanning private equity companies, venture capitalists, direct angel investments, real estate, and public stocks.

context.quote: Well, my brother and I started even a software company before that, and we went ahead to at the same time and we sold both of them.
context.claim: Hyatt reports that he and his brother started two software companies and sold both.

context.quote: So we just bootstrapped it in the beginning, which was incredibly beneficial to us later when we sold the company.
context.claim: Hyatt says the company discussed as BlueCat was initially bootstrapped and was later sold.

context.quote: We made the world's first, they called it 1U rack-mountable DNS server.
context.claim: Hyatt describes BlueCat's early product as what they called the world's first 1U rack-mountable DNS server.

context.quote: you know, I'm invested in a company in Canada called Top Hat, doing amazing.
context.claim: Hyatt states that he is personally invested in Canadian education-technology company Top Hat and describes it as doing well.

context.quote: 25% of people are never going back to the office and I could be 50.
context.claim: During the pandemic-era interview, Hyatt predicted that 25%, and possibly as many as 50%, of people would never return to office work.

context.quote: The digital transformation that would have naturally happened over seven to 10 years is happening in one year because it has to.
context.claim: During the pandemic-era interview, Hyatt said digital transformation had compressed from an expected seven-to-ten-year process into one year.

context.quote: I've committed my time to two or three entrepreneurs and two or three businesses where I sit on the board, I give my time, I give my opinion, and I lean in.
context.claim: Hyatt says he has concentrated his time in two or three entrepreneurs and businesses through board participation and active advice.

context.quote: And there's times when I can do the whole round on my own, but I pull back and I bring in my friends who can also help.
context.claim: Hyatt says he sometimes has capacity to fund a whole round but brings in helpful co-investors instead.

context.quote: You know, I do this show in New York called The Pitch.
context.claim: Hyatt reports participating in the New York-based show The Pitch, which he cites during the deal-flow discussion.

context.quote: I don't have a fund. I don't have my, I have a family office. It's me and my brother and some great partners that help me do stuff and place money.
context.claim: Hyatt distinguishes his family office, operated with his brother and partners, from a conventional investment fund.

context.quote: I mean, I invest in funds and venture capital firms and private equity and real estate.
context.claim: Hyatt says his broader allocation includes funds, venture-capital firms, private equity, and real estate.

context.quote: we have a foundation and our foundation by charter funds charities directly
context.claim: Hyatt states that his family has a foundation whose charter calls for directly funding charities.

context.quote: Our guest today built and sold two very successful software companies. He is an investor on the hit podcast, The Pitch, and the host of the new Business Unplanned It podcast. He sits on the board of advisors of Georgian Partners, one of Canada's leading venture capital firms.
context.claim: The host reports that Michael Hyatt built and sold two software companies, invests on The Pitch, hosts Business Unplanned It, and sits on Georgian Partners' advisory board.

context.quote: Well, I've been on their advisory board now for, gosh, seven years.
context.claim: Hyatt says he had served on Georgian Partners' advisory board for about seven years at the time of the interview.

context.quote: I get to invest directly into companies. I get to invest alongside Georgian. I also get to invest alongside a large private equity firm like Madison Dearborn.
context.claim: Hyatt says his investment activity includes direct company investments and investments alongside Georgian Partners and Madison Dearborn.

context.quote: And I even have a couple of investments in fund to funds, which actually invest in a lot of different VCs.
context.claim: Hyatt says he has investments in funds of funds that invest across multiple venture-capital firms.

context.quote: I know sales was natural to me and Richard coding was natural to him. He's a brilliant coder, my brother, and tech guy.
context.claim: Hyatt describes himself as sales-oriented and his brother Richard as the coder and technologist in their founding team.

context.quote: So my dad convinced him to start coding for this engineering software, which started our first company. And then I came in as a sales guy.
context.claim: Hyatt says his brother's engineering-software work started their first company and that Hyatt joined as its salesperson.

context.quote: No, my brother was the designer and product guy. I was just pure sales.
context.claim: Hyatt describes his role in the early company as sales and his brother's role as product and design.

context.quote: I had a notepad, that book and a pen and a phone and all day I would just dial, dial, dial, nine hours a day.
context.claim: Hyatt recalls spending nine-hour days manually cold-calling prospective customers during the company's early sales effort.

context.quote: We had no money. We had no brand. We had no help. We had no VC. We had no investment. Nothing. Zero.
context.claim: Hyatt says the company began without venture capital, other investment, brand recognition, or institutional help.

context.quote: I was a very, very sick child, like terminally ill child. I had multiple surgeries for the first 10 years of my life. I spent in and out of hospital.
context.claim: Hyatt says severe childhood illness and multiple surgeries shaped his early life.

context.quote: it's just that I was incredibly driven to survive and it never stopped.
context.claim: Hyatt attributes his enduring personal drive to the survival instinct formed during his childhood illness.

context.quote: And I've invested in a company in Mars in Toronto that is trying to best spoke to your DNA.
context.claim: Hyatt stated that he had invested in a Toronto MaRS-based company working on DNA-personalized treatment.

context.quote: We actually have a family office in the Yorkville area.
context.claim: Hyatt says his family office is located in Toronto's Yorkville area.

context.quote: Yeah, so we have an investment officer, we have a chief financial officer, and we have someone ahead of legal. And then we have people in finance looking at things all day.
context.claim: Hyatt says the family office has investment, finance and legal personnel.

context.quote: We have three buckets. We invest in stocks, in private equity, and venture capital as bucket number two. And then the last one, we try to buy companies or invest very significant portions into companies.
context.claim: Hyatt describes the family office's allocation approach as public stocks, private equity and venture capital, plus acquisitions or significant company stakes.

context.quote: So my brother, Richard, who built Bluecat with me comes in very technically, I come in very business
context.claim: Hyatt says he built BlueCat with his brother Richard and characterizes their respective contributions as business and technical.

context.quote: in the 90s in a recession and my brother And my parents, we all started a software company in the engineering world because my father was an engineer
context.claim: Hyatt says that during the 1990s recession he, his brother and his parents started an engineering-oriented software company; the company is not named in this passage.

context.quote: I'm one of the founding partners.
context.claim: Hyatt says he is one of the founding partners of the Creative Destruction Lab at the University of Toronto.

context.quote: I'm a very much big long term believer in the United States.
context.claim: Hyatt describes himself as a strong long-term believer in the United States.

context.quote: I'm an immigrant to Canada.
context.claim: Hyatt says he is an immigrant to Canada.

context.quote: I know this because when you travel around the world. What do you see? You see McDonald's, Starbucks, Disney, and like rap music
context.claim: Hyatt supports his view of US business strength by pointing to the global reach of American brands and culture.

context.quote: The company is called Data Stealth. It's in Mississauga. And they have a lot of really strong intellectual property. They're very good guys. And I'm not the CEO and I don't want to be a CEO again. I'm there as a supportive role to help them.
context.claim: Hyatt says Data Stealth is a Mississauga company and describes his own relationship as a supportive, non-CEO role.

context.quote: But we make an investment because when we look into the future, we think like, can Richard and I materially with our skills help that company?
context.claim: Hyatt says he and Richard made an investment based partly on whether their skills could materially help the company.

context.quote: Listen, the company is growing nicely. It's nicely profitable. We've never taken on an investor. We have no debt.
context.claim: Hyatt reports that Data Stealth was growing, profitable, investor-free, and debt-free at the time of the interview.

context.quote: Yes, BlueCat was profitable. We took our first investment.
context.claim: Hyatt says BlueCat was already profitable when it accepted its first investment.

context.quote: Well, no, this was back in 05 and I was 5 million in sales and a million profit, which is incredible if you think about it.
context.claim: Hyatt reports that in 2005 BlueCat had $5 million in sales and $1 million in profit.

context.quote: Yeah, and listen, I have an investment right now that had that issue, and now it's actually working the same way.
context.claim: Hyatt reports having a current investment whose economics improved after facing a scale-related profitability issue, without naming the company in this passage.

context.quote: Yeah, that was Diadem. We started with my family. My brother was the coder. My dad was the product manager engineer.
context.claim: Hyatt said Diadem began as a family venture in which his brother coded and his father served as product-manager engineer.

context.quote: you know there was really no vc community no way to get money or anything like that so we stayed profitable early on we built we just built up and eventually sold that business but the same time we started blue cat that was another crazy experience
context.claim: Hyatt said the family built the first business profitably without an available VC community, eventually sold it, and started BlueCat during the same period.

context.quote: We took some, but we always remained in majority control with the company, which was the strange thing.
context.claim: Hyatt said the company accepted some outside financing while its founders retained majority control.

context.quote: No, no. There's DNS security, which is one thing. It's really network infrastructure.
context.claim: Hyatt characterized BlueCat's core product as network infrastructure rather than cybersecurity.

context.quote: So I actually, the cybersecurity thing, my brother and I bought another company two years ago, 18 months ago, called Data Stealth.
context.claim: Hyatt said that he and his brother had bought DataStealth roughly 18 months to two years before the interview.

context.quote: So I am into the cybersecurity business today. I'm going for a three-peat right now.
context.claim: Hyatt described himself as currently building in cybersecurity and pursuing a third entrepreneurial success.

context.quote: And it's one of the reasons we set up a family office is to create a institution that gets them working in the office and gets them working on deals and understanding money and all that kind of stuff.
context.claim: Hyatt said one reason the family established its office was to transmit deal and financial knowledge to the next generation.

context.quote: I've surrounded myself with a really good chief investment officer, Elmer Kim. And I think a bunch of people know him on Bay Street. He's very experienced. And I have Brett Gladstone as our CFO and David Ladner as our lawyer.
context.claim: Hyatt identified Elmer Kim as the family office's chief investment officer, Brett Gladstone as CFO, and David Ladner as lawyer.

context.quote: Our true allocation is kind of like a third in stocks, a third in private equity with more private equity and small venture capital. And then a third is really buying companies and doing massive investments.
context.claim: Hyatt described the family office's approximate allocation as one-third public stocks, one-third predominantly private equity with some venture capital, and one-third company acquisitions or major direct investments.

context.quote: We're trying to buy companies. That's what we're doing.
context.claim: Hyatt said the family office actively seeks to acquire companies.

context.quote: I work with Northleaf because they were on the board of Blue Cat and I just really liked them as people. They asked me to work with them and I said I'd really like to.
context.claim: Hyatt said his Northleaf relationship followed its service on BlueCat's board and a subsequent invitation to work with the firm.

context.quote: For a long time, I didn't like Bitcoin. And even though I owned it, I've owned it for a long time.
context.claim: Hyatt said he had owned Bitcoin for a long time despite longstanding reservations about it.

context.quote: I think the safest way to buy it is probably on one of the ETFs and sit and hold it.
context.claim: Hyatt said he considered an ETF followed by long-term holding the safest way to obtain Bitcoin exposure.

context.quote: I still don't like it, but do I think it's a necessary evil to own some of it? I think so.
context.claim: Hyatt characterized a limited Bitcoin holding as a necessary portfolio hedge despite his dislike of the asset.

context.quote: Well, the Creative Destruction Lab is an incredible place. It was started by IJ Agrawal, and I was one of the first people to invest and start. I was with the original seven guys, and I'm very proud of that.
context.claim: Hyatt says he was among the original seven people involved in starting and supporting Creative Destruction Lab.

context.quote: Investments as in it was a donation, so it's not a monetary thing for me.
context.claim: Hyatt clarifies that his Creative Destruction Lab contribution was a donation rather than a monetary investment made for returns.

context.quote: We were the first that I've ever seen to really, really get into AI. I mean, I'm talking 2014, 15.
context.claim: Hyatt recalls Creative Destruction Lab engaging deeply with AI around 2014–2015.

context.quote: It's amazing. I think it's a lot of students that are all in their twenties and like 20 and 21 years old over at data stealth, our cybersecurity company
context.claim: Hyatt describes DataStealth as “our cybersecurity company,” indicating an operating relationship with it.

context.quote: I did a couple of years of the Next Gen Den.
context.claim: Hyatt says he participated in Next Gen Den for a couple of years.

context.quote: But the second thing I do is if I'm invested in a fund and I get their fund quarterly statements, I run it through and have it scored and I put it right back at them.
context.claim: Hyatt says he invests in funds and uses AI to analyze their quarterly statements.

context.quote: Then I start asking questions and drilling in and drilling in. And then I can score it really quickly and figure out right away if I should take that phone call.
context.claim: Hyatt describes an AI-assisted, question-driven scoring process for deciding which company pitches merit a call.

context.quote: So I started a software company in the 90s with my brother
context.claim: Michael says he started a software company with his brother in the 1990s.

context.quote: And Richard is this. genius developer like he was better than 100 developers together and then there was me and I could sell and we just kind of squeezed our brains together and He developed and I sold.
context.claim: Michael describes an early division of responsibilities in which his brother Richard developed software and Michael handled sales.

context.quote: My dad forced my brother to code for him. to do risk assessment. I just come out of university. So I would dial for dollars and my brother would code. And my dad would be the product manager.
context.claim: Michael says the early family software business combined his sales work, his brother's coding, and his father's product-management role in risk assessment.

context.quote: We just didn't raise, we stayed in the majority in our companies, which was the rare thing.
context.claim: Michael says he and his co-founders did not raise substantial outside financing and retained majority ownership in their companies.

context.quote: Sold both the companies is, it's a little bit of a nuance, but actually I'm still on the board of Blue Cat and I'm still a significant shareholder, but I sold the majority.
context.claim: Michael says that, at the time of the interview, he remained a Blue Cat board member and significant minority shareholder after selling majority control.

context.quote: my heart after so long wasn't in it anymore at the same level. I owe it to the staff. I owe it to the shareholders at some point. You make a broader decision.
context.claim: Michael says his decision to relinquish majority control reflected reduced personal engagement and duties to Blue Cat's staff and shareholders.

context.quote: We had people buying our DNS boxes because they desperately needed them.
context.claim: Michael describes customer purchases driven by urgent need as Blue Cat's product-market-fit signal.

context.quote: One of my great investments past couple of years, I invested in a... 22 year old who was a student at the CDL. who wasn't even in the CDL.
context.claim: Michael says he personally invested in a 22-year-old CDL student whom he regarded as one of his strong recent investments.

context.quote: Entrepreneurs I work with you'll find out that I have very candid early conversations with them.
context.claim: Michael describes candid early conversations as part of how he works with entrepreneurs.

context.quote: I drill into the math. I love math. I love... you know, you see where they're going.
context.claim: Michael says his work with entrepreneurs includes close examination of their quantitative trajectory.

context.quote: If you have investors, over communicate with them, bring them into your process.
context.claim: Michael advises founders to communicate frequently and involve investors in their decision process during difficult conditions.

context.quote: If you have advisors, decide who are your best advisor or advisors, no more than two people, and really try to get deep and narrow with that advisor.
context.claim: Michael advises founders to concentrate on no more than two deeply engaged advisors.

context.quote: TORONTO , June 25, 2020 /CNW/ - BMO has today introduced a new podcast dedicated to Canadian businesses.
context.claim: BMO reported on June 25, 2020 that it had introduced a podcast dedicated to Canadian businesses.

context.quote: Entrepreneur, investor, and co-founder of BlueCat, Michael Hyatt , has joined as the host of Business Unplanned .
context.claim: BMO identified Michael Hyatt as an entrepreneur, investor, BlueCat co-founder, and host of Business Unplanned.

context.quote: Business Unplanned will feature six episodes and be available on bmo.com/BusinessUnplanned as well as on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and Google Podcasts.
context.claim: BMO reported that Business Unplanned was planned as a six-episode podcast distributed through BMO and major podcast platforms.

context.quote: In the sixth episode of BMO Financial Group 's #BusinessUnplanned podcast, Janet Zuccarini (CEO & owner of Gusto 54 Restaurant Group) and I discuss how important it is for business owners to understand data and use it to their competitive advantage.
context.claim: In this first-person post, Hyatt reported participating with Janet Zuccarini in the sixth episode of BMO's Business Unplanned podcast.

context.quote: Hyatt is the co-founder of BlueCat, which was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, of Chicago, IL. He serves as a director of BlueCat, ranks as one of Canada’s top entrepreneurs, and is known as a technology visionary.
context.claim: The Toronto Metropolitan University profile reports that Hyatt co-founded BlueCat, that BlueCat was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, and that he continued to serve as a BlueCat director.

context.quote: Michael is also a weekly business commentator on CBC and was a celebrated “Dragon” on CBC’s online Dragons’ Den.
context.claim: The profile describes Hyatt as a weekly CBC business commentator and a former Dragon on CBC's online Dragons' Den.

context.quote: He is the Host of BMO’s Unplanned Business podcast to help small businesses and an investor on the hit Spotify podcast “The Pitch”.
context.claim: The profile reports that Hyatt hosts BMO's Unplanned Business podcast and participates as an investor on The Pitch.

context.quote: Michael is a Founding Partner and Fellow at the Rotman School of Management’s prestigious Creative Destruction Lab and sits on the CEO Board of Advisors of Georgian Partners, one of Canada’s leading venture capital firms.
context.claim: The profile reports that Hyatt is a founding partner and fellow at Creative Destruction Lab and sits on Georgian Partners' CEO Board of Advisors.

context.quote: He was also recently named Entrepreneur in Residence (EIR) at Blakes, one of the most successful law firms in the country.
context.claim: The profile reports that Hyatt had recently been named entrepreneur in residence at Blakes, without supplying an exact date.

context.quote: Michael and Vanessa are active investors and philanthropists who are part of the Hyatt Family Foundation. The foundation focuses on women’s health, critical hospital research and sponsorship of underprivileged minorities.
context.claim: The profile jointly describes Michael and Vanessa Hyatt as active investors and philanthropists associated with the Hyatt Family Foundation and reports the foundation's areas of focus.

context.quote: Michael Hyatt is a serial entrepreneur and active investor. He is the co-founder of BlueCat, (acquired by Madison Dearborn Partners), and previously co-founded Dyadem (acquired by IHS).
context.claim: The profile describes Hyatt as an active investor who co-founded BlueCat and Dyadem, both subsequently acquired.

context.quote: Michael Hyatt has invested in 1 startup on The Pitch, deploying $50K in Consumer Tech, Marketplace.
context.claim: The profile reports that Hyatt deployed $50,000 into one consumer-technology marketplace startup through The Pitch.

context.quote: Consumer Tech How Much Do You Trust Your Barista? $50K · SAFE · $6M post-money cap
context.claim: The profile reports a $50,000 SAFE investment associated with “How Much Do You Trust Your Barista?” at a $6 million post-money cap.

context.quote: BlueCat Networks, a Toronto-based provider of enterprise-class IP Address Management (IPAM) platforms, has raised a $11m first equity financing.
context.claim: FinSMEs reported on November 2, 2009 that BlueCat raised an $11 million first equity financing.

context.quote: The round was led by Bridgescale Partners, a California-based investment firm providing equity to high growth information technology companies.
context.claim: FinSMEs reported that Bridgescale Partners led BlueCat's financing round.

context.quote: As stated by Michael Hyatt, CEO and co-founder of the company, whose IP Address Management (IPAM) platforms as well as Domain Name System (DNS) and Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) solutions have been deployed to meet the rising IP management demands of government, military and both medium and large enterprises worldwide, BlueCat Networks will use the proceeds to further enhance its product line and continue the rapid expansion of its global distribution network.
context.claim: The report identifies Hyatt as BlueCat's CEO and co-founder and says BlueCat planned to use the proceeds for product enhancement and global distribution expansion.

context.quote: Hyatt, 48, co-founded and sold two software companies — Dyadem and BlueCat Networks — before launching the Hyatt Family Office in 2017.
context.claim: CNBC reported in 2022 that Hyatt co-founded and sold Dyadem and BlueCat Networks before launching Hyatt Family Office in 2017.

context.quote: Today, the Hyatt Family Office has a diversified portfolio, aiming for a third of its assets to be invested in stocks, a third in real estate and a third in venture capital and private equity. His goal is returns of 8% a year.
context.claim: CNBC reported that Hyatt Family Office targeted equal allocations to stocks, real estate, and venture capital/private equity, with an 8% annual-return goal.

context.quote: Hyatt said that one of his early family office investments was in a juice start-up. He studied the numbers, got to the know the founder and did deep information dives on the juice business before investing. Other sophisticated investors were also buying in. The company went bankrupt less than a year after he invested.
context.claim: CNBC reported that an early Hyatt Family Office investment in a juice startup failed within a year despite Hyatt's diligence and participation by other sophisticated investors.

context.quote: He mainly chooses funds where the founders also have substantial capital at risk and that are largely closed to medium-sized or small investors.
context.claim: CNBC reported that Hyatt mainly selects funds whose founders have substantial personal capital at risk and that have restricted access.

context.quote: Hyatt said he rarely touches his stock portfolio, as tempting as it is with wildly gyrating markets and rising interest rates. He said the family office largely buys Vanguard ETF's, along with a handful of his favorite stocks, which include Google, Microsoft and Apple.
context.claim: CNBC reported that Hyatt rarely trades the family office's stock portfolio and primarily uses Vanguard ETFs alongside selected technology stocks.

context.quote: Michael and Richard Hyatt have acquired a majority stake in Mississauga-based DataStealth, an enterprise cybersecurity firm that helps banks and hospitals protect their data.
context.claim: The article reports that Michael and Richard Hyatt acquired a majority stake in DataStealth.

context.quote: For the brothers—both successful Canadian tech entrepreneurs-turned-investors who previously built, scaled, sold, and exited Toronto-based Dyadem and BlueCat in deals totalling more than $1 billion—the transaction marks a return to operations.
context.claim: The article identifies the brothers as Canadian technology entrepreneurs turned investors who previously built and exited Dyadem and BlueCat.

context.quote: The Hyatt brothers’ majority stake investment closed earlier this month. Hyatt declined to disclose the price tag.
context.claim: The November 1, 2023 article reports that the majority-stake investment closed earlier that month and that its price was undisclosed.

context.quote: Hyatt has become executive chairman, and plans to focus his attention on DataStealth’s sales and go-to-market efforts, while Richard, who has also joined the board, is working with the startup’s engineering team.
context.claim: The article reports that Michael Hyatt became DataStealth's executive chairman with a focus on sales and go-to-market efforts, while Richard joined its board.

context.quote: Over the next few years, Hyatt said that their focus will be on scaling DataStealth’s business without taking on additional outside capital.
context.claim: The article reports that Hyatt planned to scale DataStealth without additional outside capital over the following few years.

context.quote: Michael Hyatt is a Canadian entrepreneur and investor recognized for his significant contributions to the technology sector. He co-founded BlueCat Networks, a company specializing in DNS security and management, which was acquired by Madison Dearborn Partners in 2017. Prior to BlueCat, he co-founded Dyadem, a software company that was acquired by IHS in 2011.
